newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Moves by Serb hardliners condemned as illegal.
newsitem.headline: Moves by Serb hardliners condemned as illegal.

text.p: Bosnian Serb President Biljana Plavsic won international and popular support on Saturday in her power struggle with diehard hardliners threatening to derail peace efforts.

The United States and other Western governments said hardliners were flouting the constitution and the Dayton peace agreement for Bosnia by ignoring Plavsic's decision to dissolve the Bosnian Serb parliament two days ago.

U.S. envoy Robert Gelbard said Plavsic had acted legally and said the conflict, pitting the Serb Republic's president against hardliners loyal to indicted war criminal Radovan Karadzic, would be raised at a NATO summit in Madrid on Sunday.
"These problems will be on the agenda. They must be solved at once in keeping with the law and Dayton," Gelbard said after meeting Plavsic in the northern town of Banja Luka.
Gelbard later lobbied Plavsic's rival, Momcilo Krajisnik, the Serb member of Bosnia's joint presidency, to step back from an increasingly tense stand-off.
Krajisnik said after the talks that he planned to meet Plavsic on Sunday in the eastern town of Bijeljina to defuse the crisis.
Thousands of people demonstrated in support of Plavsic in Banja Luka for the second day running as hardliners held an assembly session that internatinal envoys dismissed as illegal.
The hardliners in Karadzic's party failed to secure a two thirds majority needed to launch a recall vote against Plavsic and ended up amending laws to suit their purposes.
The new law allowed a majority of deputies present to call for Plavsic's removal in a referendum.
"What kind of an asesmbly do you have if you change the law when you don't have a majority?" Carlos Westendorp, the international High Representative to Bosnia, told Reuters.
The move was a "a sign that they are not at ease", Westendorp said.
The ruling Serb Democratic Party (SDS) also moved to strip Plavsic of authority as commander-in-chief by radically altering a defence council advising the president.

The SDS said Krajisnik and other government officials would now sit on the supreme defence council which would be allowed to take decisions "in the absence" of the president. International mediators were concerned that two governments were emerging, one in Banja Luka, and one directed by Karadzic in Pale, outside Sarajevo.
No shots have been fired so far in the feud but the NATO-led peace force stepped up patrols in Serb territory to ensure no violence broke out.
The feud between Plavsic and Karadzic's circle erupted a week ago when she demanded the suspension of the powerful interior minister, Dragan Kijac, a long-time Karadzic loyalist.
Plavsic delivered scathing attacks against Karadzic and his associates, accusing them of running "shameful" smuggling deals at the expense of ordinary Serbs living in abject poverty.
The hardliners were trying to isolate Plavsic, relying on their control of a heavily-armed police force and official media.
Plavsic's criticism has struck a chord among many ordinary Serbs, especially in Banja Luka, which has long resented the civilian leadership residing in the mountain village of Pale.
Plavsic was a loyal deputy to Karadzic during the 1992-95 Bosnian war and supported his "ethnic cleansing" campaign against Moslems and Croats.
Although she remains a nationalist ideologue, Western envoys say she has shown willingness to abide by the Dayton accords to end the Serbs' isolation and obtain reconstruction aid.
Karadzic, twice indicted by a U.N. war crimes tribunal, was forced to step down as president last year under heavy international pressure.
He has continued to pull strings behind the scenes but his blatant intervention against Plavsic had angered the international community and threatened to backfire, diplomats said.
